det.desc: This striking, authentic Lozi lidded food bowl is a premier example of mid-to-late 20th-century African utilitarian art. Historically used to serve prepared meats and vegetables while keeping them warm, these bowls are highly prized today by collectors of global folk art, ethnographic artifacts, and organic mid-century modern design. The piece displays incredible, traditional craftsmanship. The thin, stepped inner lip of the lid is meticulously carved to form a flush, interlocking seal with the base. Inside, the continuous, rhythmic adze gouge marks remain clearly visible across the interior walls, proving it was hollowed entirely by hand rather than turned on a mechanical lathe. Silversmiths in Newburyport, Massachusetts, often crafted decorative serving pieces like this to bring traditional elegance into everyday middle-class homes. They were made during the mid-20th century to serve sweets, nuts, or small candies during formal gatherings and family celebrations. Craftsmen created these pieces by stamping base metal alloys with heavy hydraulic presses before applying a fine layer of silver plate and detailed hand-buffing. Middle-class families used them on coffee tables, sideboards, and dining tables during holidays and special visits. Over time, as formal entertaining declined and modern stainless steel became popular for daily use, these decorative silver-plated dishes transitioned from dining tables to enclosed display cabinets.

rows.t: TOULOUSE LAUTREC RARE 1954 LITHO PRINT FRENCH EXHBT POSTER AT MOULIN ROUGE 1892

det.desc: DESCRIPTION: 1954 TOULOUSE-LAUTREC “OEUVRE GRAPHIQUE” — GALERIE DES PONCHETTES, NICE — MOURLOT LITHOGRAPHIC EXHIBITION POSTER An especially interesting piece from this collection: the 1954 lithographic exhibition poster for Oeuvre graphique de Toulouse-Lautrec at the Galerie des Ponchettes in Nice, France. The exhibition was held from January 30 through March 15, 1954 at Galerie des Ponchettes, 77 Quai des États-Unis, Nice, and was devoted to Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec’s graphic work. The official City of Nice heritage record identifies the exhibition poster as a 1954 production by Mourlot in Paris. This particular example was purchased at the exhibition itself in 1954 and has remained with the same six-piece group of Toulouse-Lautrec lithographs acquired there. THE IMAGE The poster incorporates Toulouse-Lautrec’s imagery from Au Moulin Rouge, featuring La Goulue and her sister, together with the exhibition typography and information for the Galerie des Ponchettes. Rather than simply reproducing one of Lautrec’s commercial posters, this sheet was specifically created to announce the 1954 Nice retrospective, making it an artifact of the exhibition itself. MOURLOT & MID-CENTURY FRENCH
